The patient presented with progressive jaundice, dark stools, lethargy and lightheadedness. Examination showed a pale, deeply icteric, afebrile patient with tachycardia (HR 92) and preserved systolic BP (115 mmHg) — the combination of pallor plus jaundice immediately suggested haemolysis rather than isolated hepatobiliary disease.

History was informative by its negatives: no abdominal pain, no pale/clay-coloured stools (arguing against obstructive jaundice), and a previous cholecystectomy (consistent with prior pigment gallstones from chronic red-cell turnover).

Investigations confirmed a haemolytic process: haemoglobin 45 g/L (severe anaemia), LDH 1214 U/L, haptoglobin <0.3 g/L (undetectable), total bilirubin 61 µmol/L with 72% unconjugated fraction, and a marked reticulocytosis of 261.7 ×10^9/L (23.7%). Lactate was 4.2 mmol/L, reflecting tissue hypoxia from the anaemia and explaining the lethargy and lightheadedness. The robust reticulocyte response excluded an aplastic (parvovirus B19) crisis.

The peripheral blood film showed reticulocytosis, spherocytes and reactive neutrophilia. Spherocytic haemolysis narrows the differential to autoimmune haemolytic anaemia versus hereditary spherocytosis (and, less commonly, drug-induced or microangiopathic haemolysis — but no schistocytes were seen and there was no thrombocytopenia/purpura reported).

The decisive test was the direct antiglobulin test: IgG 2+ and complement C3d 5+, with a panreactive indirect antiglobulin test and no underlying alloantibodies. A positive DAT with IgG (± C3d) plus spherocytes, high LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and reticulocytosis is diagnostic of warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Hereditary spherocytosis is excluded by the strongly positive DAT, and the absence of any lifelong history of jaundice or anaemia.

The dark stools are explained by increased bile-pigment/stercobilin load from massive haemolysis rather than melaena or biliary obstruction, given the unconjugated (not conjugated) bilirubinaemia, absence of pale stools, absence of abdominal pain, and no evidence of blood loss as the driver of the anaemia.

Secondary-cause screening (ANA, serum protein electrophoresis, HIV/hepatitis serology, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly) was requested but unavailable in this case; warm AIHA is idiopathic in roughly half of cases, but an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder, autoimmune disease, drug or viral trigger must still be sought.

Management requires urgent admission: transfusion with "least incompatible" blood (cross-matching is confounded by the panreactive autoantibody), high-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 1–1.5 mg/kg), folic acid supplementation, VTE prophylaxis, and monitoring for complications; rituximab or splenectomy is reserved for steroid-refractory disease.
